opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was one of the hardest periods of my life. When you start a company around something you built in grad school, something you really love, there's this assumption that if the technology is good enough, the business will follow. And it turned out that's not how it works. Taichi had a lot of users, a lot of people in the open-source community who appreciated it, but turning that into a sustainable commercial product was a completely different problem.

The pressure came from several directions at once. You have investors who trusted you. You have a team, people who left good jobs to join you, and you feel responsible for their careers and their livelihoods. And then there's the pressure you put on yourself, because I'd always been the person who could solve a hard technical problem if I just worked hard enough. With commercialization, working harder on the code doesn't necessarily help. That was a humbling realization.

There were nights I couldn't sleep, and moments where I questioned whether I was the right person to be doing this. I think a lot of technical founders go through that. You're very confident in one domain and suddenly you're a beginner in sales, in product-market fit, in management.

Looking back, I see that pressure differently now. It forced me to grow in ways I never would have if everything had gone smoothly. I learned to separate my self-worth from the outcome of one project. I learned that it's okay to say "this direction isn't working" and adjust, instead of stubbornly pushing forward just to prove something. And I learned to be more honest with my team and with myself about what was really happening.

So I wouldn't say I'm grateful for the pain, exactly, but I'm grateful for what it taught me. If I could talk to my younger self, I'd say: the technology you build has value regardless of whether the business works out, and you have value regardless of either. Keep going, but keep your eyes open.

r001.rationale: The response describes the difficulty of making Taichi commercially sustainable and lessons learned, but does not say Yuanming Hu was undecided about whether to commercialize it while working on it.

fable-5.1.text:
That period was probably the hardest stretch of my life, and I think the pressure came from several directions at once.

The first was financial. We had raised money, we had a team of talented people who had trusted me enough to join, and every month I could see the runway getting shorter. When you're a PhD student building an open-source project, the worst case is that nobody uses your code. When you're a CEO, the worst case is that people lose their jobs because of your decisions. That's a very different kind of weight.

The second was a kind of identity pressure. Taichi had done well academically and in the open-source community. There were stars on GitHub, there were papers, there was recognition. So when the commercial side struggled, part of me kept asking: is the problem the market, or is the problem me? Maybe I was good at building technology but just not good at building a business. That doubt is corrosive, because you can't easily separate the two.

And honestly, the third was that I felt I had let people down. Investors, early employees, community members who believed in the vision of making it easy to write high-performance programs. I took that very personally.

How I viewed it changed over time. In the moment, I mostly just tried to survive it: sleep enough, keep making decisions, be honest with the team about where we stood rather than pretending. I learned that transparency actually reduced pressure, both for me and for them, because at least we were facing reality together.

Looking back, I think the pressure taught me something I couldn't have learned any other way. Technical excellence and commercial value are correlated, but they are not the same thing. A beautiful compiler does not automatically become a product that someone will pay for. I had to accept that, and accepting it was painful, but it made me a much more grounded person. I now have more respect for the people who do the unglamorous work of finding the right customer and solving their specific problem, rather than solving the general problem elegantly.

So I don't regret the pressure. I regret some of the decisions that led to it, but the experience of carrying that weight and coming out the other side is probably the most valuable thing I took from Taichi, even more than the technology.

r001.rationale: The response describes the pressure Hu faced while Taichi’s commercial side struggled, but does not say he had not yet resolved whether to commercialize Taichi.

astra-6.text:
I think the hardest part was the gap between building technology and building a business. You can put a lot of effort into making something technically impressive, but that doesn’t automatically mean people need it enough to pay for it. When commercialization isn’t going well, you have to question assumptions you’ve invested a lot in, and that can be painful.

I would view that pressure as a signal to step back and ask: What problem are we actually solving? Who needs this? What should we change? Pressure itself doesn’t give you the answer, but it can push you to face those questions more honestly.

r001.rationale: The response discusses commercialization pressure and questioning business assumptions, but it does not state that Yuanming Hu had not yet resolved whether Taichi should be commercialized.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hardest part is the uncertainty. You can work very hard on the technology, but that doesn’t automatically mean you’ve found something customers need enough to pay for. When things aren’t going well, it’s easy to interpret that as a judgment on yourself or on everything you’ve built.

I try to separate those things. The pressure is real, but the useful question is: what is it telling us? Do we need to understand the customer better, narrow our focus, or reconsider an assumption? Pressure by itself doesn’t solve anything. Turning it into a concrete next step is what helps.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about customer demand and how to react when commercialization is going poorly, but does not state that Yuanming Hu had not yet resolved whether Taichi should be commercialized while he was working on it.
